sentences.text: Saichania was a medium-sized herbivorous ankylosaurid dinosaur that lived in Mongolia and China.
This animal measured between 5 and 7 meters long and weighed from 1.4 to 2.0 metric tons.
The holotype skull, which is the specimen the species is based on, was broad, measuring 455 millimeters in length and 480 millimeters in width.
The atlas and axis vertebrae of Saichania are fused together.
The neck was protected by two rings of six rectangular osteoderms each.
The first fossils were discovered in the early 1970s within the Baruungoyot Formation by a Polish-Mongolian expedition in the Gobi Desert near Chulsan.
The type species Saichania chulsanensis was formally named in 1977.
The genus name Saichania comes from the Mongolian word for 'beautiful', referencing the excellent preservation of the type specimen.
Saichania used a tail club to defend itself against predators such as Tarbosaurus.
It used a horny beak to bite off plants in its desert habitat and processed them in a wide hindgut.
The skull contained very complex air passages, including a scroll-like turbinate bone structure that likely helped condense and preserve exhaled moisture, similar to warm-blooded animals.
The unusually strongly ossified hard palate likely allowed it to eat tough plants.
The anatomical features suggest it lived in a hot, arid environment.
Some evidence suggests Saichania may have possessed a salt gland near its nostrils to aid survival in a desert habitat.
Maryańska classified Saichania as a member of the Ankylosauridae family, noting that its nasal cavity structure differs from all other dinosaurs.
Tianzhenosaurus and Shanxia have been proposed as potential synonyms of Saichania.
The animal lived from the Cenomanian to the Campanian stages, between 100.5 and 72.2 million years ago, and belongs to the parent group Ankylosaurinae.

In 2014, Victoria Megan Arbour debated that a previously described juvenile specimen was misleadingly reconstructed with a skull cast from the holotype and likely belonged to a different ankylosaur, possibly Pinacosaurus.
The referral of specimen PIN 3142/250 to Saichania was contested by Penkalski and Tumanova, who argued it belonged to a new species of Tarchia, T. teresae.
